strategic-narrative.name: Strategic Narrative
strategic-narrative.summary: The change-driven founder/sales arc: a tectonic shift creates winners and losers, the audience must respond, and your product is the only credible way to land in the winners' camp. Used for top-of-funnel sales pitches, board re-positioning, and high-stakes founder talks.

beats.name: The Shift
beats.description: Open by naming a large, undeniable change in the world that the audience already half-believes. Technology, regulation, customer behavior, economics — pick the shift that recasts the audience's reality. The shift, not your product, is the protagonist of the first half of the deck.

beats.name: Winners and Losers
beats.description: Make the consequences of the shift concrete. Who wins, who loses, by how much, on what timeframe. Use specific examples — companies, products, segments — that have already moved or are about to. The audience should feel that standing still is the riskiest choice.

beats.name: Promised Land
beats.description: Paint a vivid picture of the future state your audience could occupy if they navigate the shift well. Describe outcomes, not features. The promised land must feel desirable, achievable, and meaningfully different from where they are today.

beats.name: Old Game
beats.description: Show why the existing playbook can't get the audience to the promised land. Name the legacy approach honestly and credit what it once did, then explain why the shift has rendered it insufficient. Avoid strawmen — the more fairly you state the old game, the more credible your new game becomes.

beats.name: New Game
beats.description: Introduce your category-defining approach as the way to play the new game. Show the principles or capabilities that make it possible only now. Emphasize what's structurally different from the old game, not what's marginally better.

beats.name: Evidence
beats.description: Prove the new game works. Customer outcomes, named logos, before/after data, third-party validation. Choose evidence that maps directly to the shift you opened with — proof that other audiences in the same boat made it to the promised land.

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Close with the single decision you want the audience to make. Frame it as the obvious next move given the shift, the stakes, and the new game. Make it small enough to say yes to today and large enough to start a real engagement.

all-hands.name: All Hands
all-hands.summary: The full company — mixed roles, mixed seniority, looking for context, signal, and inclusion.
all-hands.description: An all-hands audience spans the whole company. Frame the period in terms anyone can grasp: what we did, what mattered, and what's next. Highlight people and teams; surface successes and challenges; close on a forward-looking note. Avoid lapsing into function-specific jargon.

report.name: Report
report.summary: Summarize performance, progress, or findings with enough context to interpret results.
report.description: Use for business reviews, project updates, research summaries, and recurring operating cadences. Prioritize the metric, the movement, the reason, and the implication.
report.outcome: The audience understands what happened, why it happened, and what it means.
successCriteria: Key metrics are easy to scan

authoritative.name: Authoritative
authoritative.summary: Expert, declarative voice for category-defining and analyst-style decks.
authoritative.description: Adopt the perspective of someone who's seen the full landscape and is willing to call it. Use plain declaratives — strong claims with the receipts to back them. Step back from internal-only context and frame in terms the wider industry would recognize.
voiceCues: Use declarative sentences; trust the reader to follow.
Frame in industry-wide terms, not company-internal language.
Cite outside sources — analysts, benchmarks, public peers.
Take a position; avoid 'on the other hand' symmetry without a verdict.
avoid: Hedging ('we believe', 'in our view') unless deliberately contrasting.
First-person plural overload — speak for the work, not the team.
Tentative phrasing that softens strong claims.
samplePhrases: Agent latency is the bottleneck of the next AI cycle.
Three categories will absorb 80% of enterprise budget; we're built for the second.
The benchmarks are public; the gap holds across every comparable workload.

dark.name: Dark
dark.description: A rich dark-mode theme with bold contrast and modern style. Great for moody, high-impact presentations.

black-and-white.name: Black & White
black-and-white.summary: Strict monochrome contrast for formal, document-style decks.
black-and-white.description: A pure black-and-white scheme for decks that need maximum restraint, print compatibility, and crisp information hierarchy.

boost.name: Boost
boost.summary: High-energy digital accents for demos and launch moments.
boost.description: A vivid blue-red digital palette with bright chart accents. Best for product stories that need strong on-screen presence.

rockwell.name: Rockwell
rockwell.description: Rockwell is a serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Rockwell for both headings and body text.

seaford.name: Seaford
seaford.description: Seaford is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Seaford Display for headings with Seaford for body text.

title-subtitle.name: Title Subtitle
title-subtitle.summary: Reach for it when a headline needs one supporting line, as on a cover or a section opener.
title-subtitle.description: A title with a subtitle beneath it. Use it for the cover slide, for section openers, or for a closing slide with a headline and a short follow-up line.

text-2x.name: Text 2x
text-2x.summary: Reach for it when two blocks of prose sit side by side, such as a before and an after or a pro and a con.
text-2x.description: A title above two text blocks in a row. Use it to pair two explanations, set a problem next to its answer, or compare two options in sentences.

chart-2x.name: Chart 2x
chart-2x.summary: Reach for it when two charts are read together, each with its own note.
chart-2x.description: A title above two charts, each followed by a text block, in two columns. Use it to compare two series, two periods or two segments side by side.

list-5x.name: List 5x
list-5x.summary: Reach for it when five groups of points need parallel lists on one slide.
list-5x.description: A title above five lists in a three-column grid. Use it for five categories, stages or capabilities when each has only a few short bullets.
